claim: Metastasis is the main cause of death in cancer patients.
source: Metastasis is the main cause of death in cancer patients but remains a poorly understood process.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific consensus about cancer mortality.

claim: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is one of the most lethal and most metastatic cancer types.
source: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is one of the most lethal and most metastatic cancer types.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about SCLC characteristics.

claim: SCLC cells normally express neuroendocrine and neuronal gene programs.
source: SCLC cells normally express neuroendocrine and neuronal gene programs but accumulating evidence indicates that these cancer cells become relatively more neuronal and less neuroendocrine as they gain the ability to metastasize.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature in the manuscript.

claim: SCLC cancer cells become relatively more neuronal and less neuroendocrine as they gain the ability to metastasize.
source: SCLC cells normally express neuroendocrine and neuronal gene programs but accumulating evidence indicates that these cancer cells become relatively more neuronal and less neuroendocrine as they gain the ability to metastasize.
evidence: This is supported by accumulating evidence referenced in the manuscript and by the authors' own data.

claim: Mouse and human SCLC cells in culture and in vivo can grow cellular protrusions that resemble axons.
source: Here we show that mouse and human SCLC cells in culture and in vivo can grow cellular protrusions that resemble axons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The formation of axon-like protrusions is controlled by multiple neuronal factors implicated in axonogenesis, axon guidance, and neuroblast migration.
source: The formation of these protrusions is controlled by multiple neuronal factors implicated in axonogenesis, axon guidance, and neuroblast migration.
evidence: This is supported by knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Disruption of axon-like protrusions impairs cell migration in culture.
source: Disruption of these axon-like protrusions impairs cell migration in culture and inhibits metastatic ability in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing reduced migration upon knockdown of pro-protrusion genes.

claim: Disruption of axon-like protrusions inhibits metastatic ability in vivo.
source: Disruption of these axon-like protrusions impairs cell migration in culture and inhibits metastatic ability in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing reduced metastasis upon knockdown of pro-protrusion genes.

claim: The co-option of developmental neuronal programs is a novel molecular and cellular mechanism that contributes to the high metastatic ability of SCLC.
source: The co-option of developmental neuronal programs is a novel molecular and cellular mechanism that contributes to the high metastatic ability of SCLC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the collective experimental data.

claim: SCLC accounts for ~15% of all lung cancers.
source: Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is a high-grade neuroendocrine cancer that accounts for ~15% of all lung cancers and causes over 200,000 deaths worldwide each year (Sabari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sabari et al., 2017.

claim: SCLC causes over 200,000 deaths worldwide each year.
source: Small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) is a high-grade neuroendocrine cancer that accounts for ~15% of all lung cancers and causes over 200,000 deaths worldwide each year (Sabari et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sabari et al., 2017.

claim: Over 60% of SCLC patients present with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis.
source: SCLC is one of the most metastatic human cancers, with over 60% of SCLC patients presenting with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis, often including liver, bone, brain, and secondary lung metastases (Nakazawa et al., 2012; Riihimäki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakazawa et al., 2012 and Riihimäki et al., 2014.

claim: SCLC metastases often include liver, bone, brain, and secondary lung metastases.
source: SCLC is one of the most metastatic human cancers, with over 60% of SCLC patients presenting with disseminated disease at the time of diagnosis, often including liver, bone, brain, and secondary lung metastases (Nakazawa et al., 2012; Riihimäki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakazawa et al., 2012 and Riihimäki et al., 2014.

claim: Genetically engineered mouse models of human SCLC recapitulate the genetics, histology, therapeutic response, and highly metastatic nature of the human disease.
source: Genetically engineered mouse models of human SCLC recapitulate the genetics, histology, therapeutic response, and highly metastatic nature of the human disease (Kwon and Berns, 2013; Gazdar et al., 2015; Rudin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kwon and Berns, 2013; Gazdar et al., 2015; and Rudin et al., 2019.

claim: Higher levels of neuronal markers such as NSE correlate with shorter survival and more metastatic disease in SCLC patients.
source: Higher levels of the neuronal markers such as NSE (neuron-specific enolase) correlate with shorter survival and more metastatic disease in SCLC patients (Carney et al., 1982; van Zandwijk et al., 1992; Dong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Carney et al., 1982; van Zandwijk et al., 1992; and Dong et al., 2019.

claim: Broad neuronal gene expression programs are enriched in metastases from mouse models of SCLC.
source: Broad neuronal gene expression programs are enriched in metastases from mouse models of SCLC, however, whether SCLC cells actually gain neuronal characteristics and whether neuronal features are key regulators of metastatic ability has not been previously characterized (Denny et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; Böttger et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Denny et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2018; and Böttger et al., 2019.

claim: Some SCLC cell lines form long cellular protrusions into cell-free spaces.
source: Unexpectedly, we noticed that cells from some SCLC cell lines (N2N1G, 16T, 6PF) derived from the Rbf/f;Trp53f/f (DKO) and Rbf/f;Trp53 f/f;p130f/f (TKO) genetically engineered mouse models form long cellular protrusions into cell-free spaces (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: SCLC cells form protrusions when they are in close contact with surrounding cancer cells.
source: We found that SCLC cells also form protrusions when they are in close contact with surrounding cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar protrusion structures extend from SCLC micro-metastases in the liver in the autochthonous TKO mouse model.
source: Finally, similar structures also extend from SCLC micro-metastases in the liver in the autochthonous TKO mouse model and after intravenous transplantations of SCLC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Protrusions are observed in subcutaneous allografts of SCLC cells.
source: Similar mixing experiments performed in subcutaneous allografts also documented the growth of protrusions by SCLC cells in vivo (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Protrusions from SCLC cells were identifiable in two out of three human SCLC PDX models.
source: Protrusions from SCLC cells were easily identifiable in two out of three PDX models (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Human NCI-H446 SCLC cells formed long protrusions into cell-free areas in 2D culture.
source: Furthermore, human NCI-H446 SCLC cells formed long protrusions into cell-free areas in the 2D culture system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E) and when grown as xenografts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Many genes classically associated with axonogenesis and axon guidance are expressed in at least subsets of primary human SCLCs.
source: We identified a list of 69 genes classically associated in the scientific literature with axonogenesis and axon guidance, and found that many of these genes are expressed in at least subsets of primary human SCLCs (George et al., 2015) (Supplementary file 2–table 2).
evidence: This is supported by data from George et al., 2015 and analysis shown in Supplementary file 2–table 2.

claim: The protrusions from murine and human SCLC cell lines uniformly expressed neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin (Tuj1).
source: The protrusions that form from murine and human SCLC cell lines uniformly expressed neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin (Tuj1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: SCLC protrusions were positive for the axonal marker TAU.
source: More importantly, these protrusions were positive for the axonal marker TAU while expression of the dendritic marker MAP2 was undetectable (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Expression of the dendritic marker MAP2 was undetectable in SCLC protrusions.
source: More importantly, these protrusions were positive for the axonal marker TAU while expression of the dendritic marker MAP2 was undetectable (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A-B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Tuj1-positive, TAU-positive protrusions were observed in vivo emanating from SCLC cells in the liver of TKO mice.
source: Tuj1positive, TAUpositive protrusions were also observed in vivo emanating from SCLC cells in the liver of TKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 29/79 (37%) human primary SCLC tumors stained moderately or strongly positive for TAU.
source: Furthermore, 29/79 (37%) human primary SCLC tumors stained moderately or strongly positive for TAU (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SCLC protrusions were often 5 to 10 times longer than the diameter of the cell body.
source: We quantified the length of protrusions and found that they were often 5 to 10 times longer than the diameter of the cell body (~8 µm) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SCLC cell lines that form protrusions displayed increased saltatory activity compared to SCLC cells that do not form protrusions.
source: Indeed, when we quantified the movement of SCLC cell along protrusions, SCLC cell lines that form protrusions (16T and N2N1G cell lines) displayed increased saltatory activity compared to SCLC cells that do not form protrusions (KP22 cell line) (Figure 2D–H and Video 2, 3, and 4).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2D-H and Videos 2-4.

claim: The velocity of SCLC cells that form protrusions was greatly increased compared to cells that do not form protrusions.
source: The velocity of SCLC cells that form protrusions was also greatly increased compared to cells that do not form protrusions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The 13-gene signature correlated more closely with the 'SCLC-N' subtype driven by the transcription factor NEUROD1.
source: In human tumors (George et al., 2015), the 13-gene signature correlated more closely with the 'SCLC-N' subtype, driven by the transcription factor NEUROD1, and both human cell line NCI-H446 and the PDX model LU86 (Saunders et al., 2015) belong to this subtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and data from George et al., 2015.

claim: The 13-gene signature correlated with high NFIB expression.
source: Notably, the 13-gene signature correlated with high NFIB expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NFIB knock-down in mouse SCLC cells reduced the formation of protrusions.
source: NFIB knock-down in mouse SCLC cells that had high NFIB levels and formed protrusions did not result in the global downregulation of the 13-gene signature, but was sufficient to reduce the formation of protrusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Overexpression of NFIB in SCLC mouse cells with low NFIB levels was not sufficient to induce the growth of protrusions.
source: Overexpression of NFIB in SCLC mouse cells with low NFIB levels and without protrusions was not sufficient to lead to the upregulation of the entire set of 13 genes or to induce the growth of protrusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,G.

claim: Knock-down of 11 of the 13 genes significantly reduced the number of protrusions with at least one shRNA.
source: Knock-down of 11 of the 13 genes significantly reduced the number of protrusions with at least one shRNA (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Knock-down of many genes involved in axon formation, axonal guidance, and neuronal migration reduced cell migration.
source: Knock-down of the many genes involved in axon formation, axonal guidance, and neuronal migration also reduced cell migration (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Inhibition of migration correlated with loss of the axon-like protrusions.
source: Quantification of cell migration showed that inhibition of migration correlated with loss of the axon-like protrusions (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Knock-down of Gap43 and Fez1 reduced the ability of SCLC cells to migrate out of 3D spheroids in Matrigel.
source: Finally, we found that knock-down of Gap43 and Fez1 reduced the ability of SCLC 16T and N2N1G cells to migrate out of 3D spheroids in Matrigel (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-G.

claim: The expression of neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin and TAU was barely detectable in non-metastatic tumors in the lungs of TKO mice 3 months after cancer initiation.
source: In support of this idea, we found that the expression of neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin and TAU was barely detectable in non-metastatic tumors in the lungs of TKO mice 3 months after cancer initiation while a majority of later stage tumors stained strongly positive for both proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: A majority of later stage tumors stained strongly positive for neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin and TAU.
source: In support of this idea, we found that the expression of neuron-specific class III beta-tubulin and TAU was barely detectable in non-metastatic tumors in the lungs of TKO mice 3 months after cancer initiation while a majority of later stage tumors stained strongly positive for both proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: GAP43 was detectable in 6/9 human SCLC metastases analyzed.
source: GAP43 was detectable in 6/9 human SCLC metastases analyzed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a significant increase of key genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal migration in metastases compared to primary tumors in a mouse model of SCLC.
source: We also found a significant increase of key genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal migration in metastases compared to primary tumors in a mouse model of SCLC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Knock-down of Gap43 and Fez1 significantly reduced the number of metastases after intravenous injection of SCLC cells.
source: Knock-down of each of these pro-protrusion factors significantly reduced the number of metastases as assessed by tumor counts at the surface of the liver 4–5 weeks after intravenous injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B and Figure 4B-C, E-H.

claim: Knock-down of Gap43 and Fez1 had no effect on subcutaneous tumor growth.
source: Knock-down of these genes had no effect on subcutaneous tumor growth suggesting that the effects on metastatic ability likely represent the disruption of phenotypes uniquely associated with the metastatic process (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Gap43 and Fez1 knock-down reduced metastatic seeding by SCLC cells in the liver 2 days after injection.
source: Quantification of GFPpositive cancer cells in the liver by flow cytometry documented a significant reduction in metastatic seeding by SCLC cells with Gap43 or Fez1 knocked-down (Figure 4J–M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4J-M and Figure 4—figure supplement 2F-I.

claim: Reduced expression of genes associated with the formation of axon-like protrusions affects early metastatic seeding of SCLC cells in the liver.
source: Thus, reduced expression of genes associated with the formation of axon-like protrusions affects early metastatic seeding of SCLC cells in the liver, which ultimately translates to reduced metastatic burden.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: SCLC cells can grow axon-like protrusions that contribute to the migratory and metastatic phenotypes of these cells.
source: Here we investigated the function of neuronal gene expression programs in metastatic SCLC. We found that SCLC cells can grow axon-like protrusions and that these protrusions contribute to the migratory and metastatic phenotypes of these cells.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the collective experimental data.

claim: A neuroendocrine-to-neuronal transition promotes metastasis of SCLC cells.
source: This study identifies a cellular mechanism by which a neuroendocrine-to-neuronal transition promotes metastasis of SCLC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing that neuronal features promote metastasis.

claim: The expression of neuronal factors in SCLC has been known for more than three decades.
source: The expression of neuronal factors in SCLC has been known for more than three decades and has been used as a marker for disease progression (Carney et al., 1982; Cutz, 1982; Broers et al., 1987; Anderson et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Axon-like protrusions may have functions beyond facilitating metastatic seeding to the liver.
source: Furthermore, these axon-like protrusions may have other functions beyond facilitating metastatic seeding to the liver, which may including facilitating SCLC cell migration within the primary tumor, intravasation into the bloodstream, and movement within the parenchyma during metastatic expansion (Shibue et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential additional functions, supported by a citation.

claim: Several other human tumor types increase the expression of neuronal programs as they become more metastatic, especially to the brain.
source: Recent evidence suggests that several other human tumor types also increase the expression of neuronal programs as they become more metastatic, especially to the brain (Wingrove et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wingrove et al., 2019.

claim: Knock-down of Dcx has little to no effect on the number of protrusions but strongly inhibits migration.
source: For instance, we found that knock-down of Dcx (coding for Doublecortin) has little to no effect on the number of protrusions but strongly inhibits migration in our 2D Matrigel assay (Figure 3A–B), thus Doublecortin may promote SCLC migration independent from an impact on protrusion formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Doublecortin may promote SCLC migration independent from an impact on protrusion formation.
source: For instance, we found that knock-down of Dcx (coding for Doublecortin) has little to no effect on the number of protrusions but strongly inhibits migration in our 2D Matrigel assay (Figure 3A–B), thus Doublecortin may promote SCLC migration independent from an impact on protrusion formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that Dcx knockdown affects migration but not protrusions.

claim: NFIB transcription factor plays a role in the up-regulation of neuronal gene programs in SCLC.
source: Existing data support a role for the NFIB transcription factor across SCLC subtypes in the up-regulation of neuronal gene programs in general and gene programs associated more specifically with axonogenesis and neuronal migration (this study and Denny et al., 2016; Semenova et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data from this study and citations to Denny et al., 2016; Semenova et al., 2016; and Wu et al., 2016.

claim: A combination of genetic and epigenetic factors likely contributes to the ability of SCLC to grow protrusions.
source: However, it is likely that a combination of genetic and epigenetic factors contributes to the ability of SCLC to grow protrusions (Qadeer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Qadeer et al., 2019.

claim: Adhesion molecules and other factors in the tumor microenvironment are likely to contribute to the formation of protrusions in vivo.
source: Adhesion molecules and other factors in the tumor microenvironment are also likely to contribute to the formation of protrusions in vivo (Guo et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2000.

claim: Targeting NFIB may help inhibit SCLC metastatic potential in the future.
source: Because NFIB is an important regulator of neuronal gene programs in SCLC cells, targeting this transcription factor may help inhibit SCLC metastatic potential in the future; one possible strategy could be the use of targeted proteolysis (Paiva and Crews, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic strategies, supported by a citation.

claim: CXCR4 contributes to the formation of axon-like protrusions.
source: Interestingly, CXCR4 also contributes to the formation of axon-like protrusions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In a recent clinical trial in SCLC patients, CXCR4 inhibition was well tolerated but did not significantly reduce disease progression.
source: In a recent clinical trial in SCLC patients, CXCR4 inhibition was well tolerated but this inhibition did not significantly reduce disease progression (Salgia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Salgia et al., 2017.

claim: The transition from a neuroendocrine state to a state where neuronal differentiation is increased may be related to the exceptional plasticity of SCLC cells.
source: More generally, the transition from a neuroendocrine state to a state where neuroendocrine differentiation is decreased but neuronal differentiation is increased may be related to the exceptional plasticity of SCLC cells (reviewed in Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Yuan et al., 2019.

claim: The epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) may play a role in SCLC.
source: The epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is thought to contribute to migration, metastasis, and resistance to treatment in many cancer contexts and may play a role in SCLC (Singh and Settleman, 2010; Cañadas et al., 2014; Krohn et al., 2014; Allison Stewart et al., 2017; O'Brien-Ball and Biddle, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Vascular mimicry may contribute to tumor growth and response to treatment in SCLC.
source: Vascular mimicry (or epithelial-to-endothelial transition (EET) Yuan et al., 2019) may also contribute to tumor growth and response to treatment in SCLC (Williamson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yuan et al., 2019 and Williamson et al., 2016.

claim: Notch-induced dedifferentiation to a non-neuroendocrine state can generate an intra-tumoral niche that protects neuroendocrine SCLC cells.
source: Similarly, Notch-induced dedifferentiation to a non-neuroendocrine state can generate an intra-tumoral niche that protects neuroendocrine SCLC cells (Lim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lim et al., 2017.

claim: An epithelial-to-neuronal transition contributes to key aspects of cancer metastasis.
source: Based on our results and recent observations in other cancers (Wingrove et al., 2019), we propose that an epithelial-to-neuronal transition contributes to key aspects of cancer metastasis.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the authors' results and a citation to Wingrove et al., 2019.

claim: SCLC cells classically grow in culture as floating spheres or aggregates.
source: To investigate SCLC migration, we developed an assay in which SCLC cells, which classically grow in culture as floating spheres or aggregates, are grown as a monolayer under Matrigel (Denny et al., 2016 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the typical culture characteristics of SCLC cells, supported by a citation.

claim: Most axonogenesis and neuronal migration genes were undetectable in a single-cell RNA-seq analysis of adult lung epithelial cells.
source: Most axonogenesis and neuronal migration genes were undetectable in a single-cell RNA-seq analysis of adult lung epithelial cells, which included neuroendocrine cell, further suggesting that these programs are turned on during tumorigenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) (Ouadah et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C from Ouadah et al., 2019.

claim: Axonal programs are gained during SCLC progression.
source: Together, these observations indicate that axonal programs are gained during SCLC progression and suggested that the protrusions from SCLC cells are axon-like.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including gene expression and immunostaining data.

claim: The protrusions from SCLC cells are axon-like.
source: Together, these observations indicate that axonal programs are gained during SCLC progression and suggested that the protrusions from SCLC cells are axon-like.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including marker expression and morphology.

claim: The protrusions from SCLC cells are very dynamic.
source: Initial observations of mouse SCLC cells showed that the protrusions were very dynamic (Figure 2D and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 2D and Video 1.

claim: The protrusions resemble cellular processes described in neuroblasts and the movement of SCLC cells along these protrusions is reminiscent of neuronal tangential migration exhibited by neuroblasts.
source: In these videos, we noticed that the protrusions resembled cellular processes that have been described in neuroblasts and with the movement of SCLC cells along these protrusions reminiscent of neuronal tangential migration exhibited by neuroblasts (Lois et al., 1996; Oudin et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2015) and interneurons (Leclech et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation supported by citations to studies on neuroblast migration.

claim: SCLC cells can generate axon-like protrusions that facilitate migration in a manner qualitatively similar to neuroblast migration during brain development.
source: Together, these results indicate that SCLC cells can generate axon-like protrusions and that these projections facilitate migration in a manner that is qualitatively similar to neuroblast migration during brain development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations of protrusion formation and cell migration.

claim: The 13 selected genes encode proteins functionally involved in diverse aspects of axon formation, axon guidance, and neuronal migration.
source: To investigate the functional importance of these axon-like protrusions and their regulation, we focused on 13 genes (out of the 69 genes selected above) that encode for proteins functionally involved in diverse aspects of axon formation, axon guidance, and neuronal migration (Supplementary file 2–table 5).
evidence: This is supported by literature searches and functional annotations.

claim: The 13 candidate genes are all expressed in at least a subset of human SCLC tumors.
source: These 13 genes are all expressed in at least a subset of human SCLC tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (data from George et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A from George et al., 2015.

claim: The 13 candidate proteins have a significant connection with biological processes related to neurogenesis and the regulation of neuron projection development.
source: STRING analysis and literature searches confirmed that these 13 candidates had a significant connection with biological processes related to neurogenesis and the regulation of neuron projection development.
evidence: This is supported by STRING analysis and literature searches.

claim: The 13 candidate proteins were not often connected with one another and thus likely contribute to distinct aspects of neuronal biological processes.
source: These proteins were not often connected with one another and thus likely contribute to distinct aspects of these biological processes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 2–table 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from STRING analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Human cell line NCI-H446 and the PDX model LU86 belong to the SCLC-N subtype.
source: In human tumors (George et al., 2015), the 13-gene signature correlated more closely with the 'SCLC-N' subtype, driven by the transcription factor NEUROD1, and both human cell line NCI-H446 and the PDX model LU86 (Saunders et al., 2015) belong to this subtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by subtype classification from George et al., 2015 and Saunders et al., 2015.

claim: The murine cell lines used to study protrusions belong to the SCLC-A subtype.
source: The murine cell lines used to study protrusions in this study are of the 'SCLC-A' subtype (driven by the transcription factor ASCL1), even though the correlation between the 13-gene signature and ASCL1 expression was weak in mouse tumors (Yang et al., 2018) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by subtype classification from Yang et al., 2018 and analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no correlation between ASCL1 and NEUROD1 expression and the ability to grow protrusions in other human cell lines.
source: We also found no correlation between ASCL1 and NEUROD1 expression and the ability to grow protrusions in other human cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 2–table 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 2–table 1.

claim: The ability to grow protrusions may exist across SCLC subtypes.
source: Thus, the ability to grow protrusions may exist across SCLC subtypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that protrusions are found in different SCLC subtypes.

claim: NFIB knock-down in mouse SCLC cells did not result in the global downregulation of the 13-gene signature.
source: NFIB knock-down in mouse SCLC cells that had high NFIB levels and formed protrusions did not result in the global downregulation of the 13-gene signature, but was sufficient to reduce the formation of protrusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: NFIB upregulation may be important in the induction of neuronal programs in SCLC cells.
source: Thus, while NFIB upregulation may be important in the induction of neuronal programs in SCLC cells, the upstream factors that control neuronal programs specifically associated with axonogenesis and migration in SCLC remain to be fully characterized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the NFIB knockdown and overexpression experiments.

claim: The upstream factors that control neuronal programs specifically associated with axonogenesis and migration in SCLC remain to be fully characterized.
source: Thus, while NFIB upregulation may be important in the induction of neuronal programs in SCLC cells, the upstream factors that control neuronal programs specifically associated with axonogenesis and migration in SCLC remain to be fully characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge based on the experimental results.

claim: Knock-down of the 13 genes rarely affected the growth of SCLC cells in culture.
source: In the 25 human SCLC cell lines analyzed in the Cancer Dependency Map project, knock-down of these 13 genes rarely affected the growth of SCLC cells in culture, consistent with these genes influencing aspects of cell physiology not related to the cell cycle (Supplementary file 2–table 7 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data from the Cancer Dependency Map project shown in Supplementary file 2–table 7 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ~50% of human primary SCLC tumors stained moderately or strongly positive for GAP43.
source: We performed immunostaining for one of these 13 proteins (GAP43) and found that ~50% of human primary SCLC tumors stained moderately or strongly positive (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), further supporting a role for neuronal programs linked to axonogenesis and migration in SCLC.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The 13-gene signature was overall more highly expressed in N2N1G cells compared to KP22 cells.
source: The 13-gene signature was overall more highly expressed in N2N1G cells, which are derived from a lymph node metastasis and grow protrusions compared to KP22 cells that do not grow protrusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: N2N1G cells are derived from a lymph node metastasis.
source: The 13-gene signature was overall more highly expressed in N2N1G cells, which are derived from a lymph node metastasis and grow protrusions compared to KP22 cells that do not grow protrusions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a statement about the origin of the N2N1G cell line.

claim: Inhibition of axonal growth reduced the development of protrusions from SCLC cells.
source: Knock-down of multiple factors normally implicated in distinct steps of axonal growth reduced the development of protrusions from SCLC cells, thus further bolstering the notion that these protrusions are similar to neuronal axons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SCLC cells with axon-like protrusions migrate in culture similar to neuroblasts.
source: Together, these data show that SCLC cells with axon-like protrusions migrate in culture similar to what has been described for neuroblasts and that disruption of these protrusions by knocking down a variety of diverse genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal migration also reduces SCLC migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the migration experiments and comparison to neuroblast migration.

claim: Disruption of protrusions by knocking down genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal migration reduces SCLC migration.
source: Together, these data show that SCLC cells with axon-like protrusions migrate in culture similar to what has been described for neuroblasts and that disruption of these protrusions by knocking down a variety of diverse genes involved in axonogenesis and neuronal migration also reduces SCLC migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The products of Gap43 and Fez1 genes are thought to regulate axonal development in distinct manners.
source: The products of these genes are thought to regulate axonal development in distinct manners but knock-down of each reduced the formation of protrusions and cell migration in culture.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about GAP43 and FEZ1 function.

claim: Knock-down of Gap43 and Fez1 reduced the formation of protrusions and cell migration in culture.
source: The products of these genes are thought to regulate axonal development in distinct manners but knock-down of each reduced the formation of protrusions and cell migration in culture.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The effects of Gap43 and Fez1 knockdown on metastatic ability likely represent the disruption of phenotypes uniquely associated with the metastatic process.
source: Knock-down of these genes had no effect on subcutaneous tumor growth suggesting that the effects on metastatic ability likely represent the disruption of phenotypes uniquely associated with the metastatic process (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that knockdown affects metastasis but not subcutaneous growth.

claim: Other phenotypes associated with neurons beyond axon-like protrusions may also contribute to the expansion and spread of SCLC cells.
source: It is likely that other phenotypes usually associated with neurons beyond these axon-like protrusions also contribute to the expansion and the spread of SCLC cells.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential additional neuronal phenotypes.

claim: Other molecular mechanisms certainly also increase the probability that a cancer cell will successfully overcome all the hurdles that limit the development of tissue destructive metastases.
source: Our data indicate that SCLC metastasis is facilitated by the development of axon-like protrusions, however other molecular mechanisms certainly also increase the probability that a cancer cell will successfully overcome all the hurdles that limit the development of tissue destructive metastases.
evidence: This is a general statement acknowledging that metastasis is a complex process with multiple mechanisms.
